html:
Nigeria is the most populous country in Africa, in West Africa between the Sahel and the Gulf of Guinea. Britain created it in 1914 by joining its northern and southern protectorates.

The land had a long history before that. The Nok culture made terracotta figures in the first millennium BCE. Later came the Hausa city-states, Kanem-Bornu around Lake Chad, the Yoruba kingdoms of Ife and Oyo, and the kingdom of Benin. In the 1800s the Sokoto Caliphate united much of the north under Islamic rule.

Britain annexed Lagos in 1861, and the Royal Niger Company traded up the river. Frederick Lugard joined the two halves in 1914 and ruled the north through its emirs, a method called indirect rule. North and south were run so differently that the country stayed divided along those lines.

After independence:

  • 1960: independence; a republic from 1963.
  • 1966: two military coups and killings of Igbo in the north.
  • 1967 to 1970: the east broke away as Biafra. The civil war ended in a famine that killed a very large number of people.
  • Oil, first found in 1956, became the country's main income.
  • 1991: the capital moved from Lagos to Abuja.
  • 1999: return to civilian rule after most years since 1966 under the army.

Nigeria also has one of Africa's great literatures, from Chinua Achebe to Wole Soyinka, the first African Nobel laureate in literature.
sum: Nigeria is the most populous country in Africa, in West Africa between the Sahel and the Gulf of Guinea. Britain created it in 1914 by joining its northern and southern protectorates.
